rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī contrasts the soul settled in worldly life with the soul settled in knowledge of God and servitude to Him.
rows.anchor: لما وصف حال من اطمأن إلى الدنيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address may be God speaking directly to the believer as an honor, as He spoke to Moses, or speaking through an angel.
rows.anchor: إكراما له كما كلم موسى عليه السلام

rows.speaker: القفال
rows.claim: Al-Qaffāl reads the imperative as a report in meaning: when the soul is tranquil, it returns to God and is told to enter among His servants and His garden.
rows.anchor: وقال القفال : هذا وإن كان أمرا في الظاهر لكنه خبر في المعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Iṭmiʾnān means settling and becoming firm.
rows.anchor: وفي كيفية هذا الاستقرار وجوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation is a soul certain of the truth, with no doubt disturbing it, as in Abraham’s request for his heart to be reassured.
rows.anchor: أن تكون متيقنة بالحق ،   فلا يخالجها شك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation is a secure soul unshaken by fear or grief; this security may come at death, resurrection, and entry into Paradise.
rows.anchor: النفس الآمنة التي لا يستفزها خوف ولا حزن

rows.speaker: أبي بن كعب
rows.claim: Ubayy ibn Kaʿb’s reading adds الآمنة, describing the soul as secure as well as tranquil.
rows.anchor: قراءة أبي بن كعب يا أيتها النفس الآمنة المطمئنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The soul’s security is realized when it hears the angelic promise not to fear or grieve and to rejoice in Paradise.
rows.anchor: ألا تخافوا ولا تحزنوا وأبشروا بالجنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurʾānic teaching and rational demonstration both show that tranquility comes only through remembering God.
rows.anchor: القرآن والبرهان تطابقا على أن هذا الاطمئنان لا يحصل إلا بذكر الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The intellect ascends through contingent causes until it reaches the Necessary Existent, the terminus of needs, and rests there.
rows.anchor: حتى ينتهي في ذلك الترقي إلى واجب الوجود لذاته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Unending human needs cannot be satisfied by finite things; only God’s limitless perfection can bring repose.
rows.anchor: فلابد في مقابلة حاجة العبد التي لا نهاية لها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rāzī describes the tranquil soul as one who seeks knowledge of God for an end beyond God, and whose intimacy, longing, life, and speech are with God.
rows.anchor: أما من آثر معرفة الله لشيء سواه فنفسه هي النفس المطمئنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This address benefits a person only when perfected in divine intellectual power or in detachment and singular devotion.
rows.anchor: لا ينتفع الإنسان به إلا إذا كان كاملا في القوة الفكرية الإلهية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qurʾān describes the self without qualification, as commanding evil, self-reproaching, and tranquil in this verse.
rows.anchor: وتارة وصفها بكونها أمارة بالسوء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The self is the reality meant by “I” when someone reports what they did, saw, heard, desired, imagined, or remembered.
rows.anchor: نفس ذاتك وحقيقتك وهي التي تشير إليها بقولك : ( أنا )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The self is not the bodily form: one can know oneself while unaware of the body, and bodily parts change while the self remains continuous.
rows.anchor: هذه البنية متبدلة الأجزاء والمشار إليه بقولك : ( أنا ) غير متبدل

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Some argue that the soul is not a body because one can apprehend the self while heedless of the body; Rāzī says his response appears in Lubāb al-Ishārāt.
rows.anchor: قال قوم إن النفس ليست بجسم لأنا قد نعقل المشار إليه

rows.speaker: آخرون
rows.claim: Others hold that the soul is a subtle, clear, luminous celestial corporeal substance unlike elemental bodies; joined to the body it makes it live, and separated it leaves the body dead.
rows.anchor: وقال آخرون : بل هو جوهر جسماني لطيف صاف بعيد عن مشابهة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the soul is incorporeal, its coming and return mean taking up and relinquishing governance; if it is a subtle body, the description is literal.
rows.anchor: يكون وصفها بالمجيء والرجوع بمعنى التدبير وتركه

rows.speaker: من القدماء
rows.claim: Some ancient thinkers argued that souls are eternal, reasoning that “return to your Lord” implies existence before the body.
rows.anchor: من القدماء من زعم أن النفوس أزلية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the address occurs at death, it supports the precedence of souls over bodies, but precedence does not prove eternity.
rows.anchor: أنه إنما يوجد عند الموت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the address occurs at resurrection, “return” means return to the Lord’s reward and reenter the body from which the soul departed.
rows.anchor: إنما يوجد عند البعث والقيامة

rows.speaker: المجسمة
rows.claim: Anthropomorphists use the directional phrase and the endpoint sense of إلى to argue that God occupies a spatial direction.
rows.anchor: المجسمة تمسكوا بقوله : { إلى ربك }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase can mean return to God’s judgment, reward, or beneficence, rather than movement toward a place.
rows.anchor: إلى حكم ربك ،   أو إلى ثواب ربك أو إلى إحسان ربك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The intellect ascends through beings and causes until it reaches the Necessary Existent, where goals and motion end.
rows.anchor: القوة العقلية بسيرها العقلي تترقى من موجود إلى موجود آخر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The soul is content with its reward, and God is pleased with the deeds it performed in worldly life.
rows.anchor: فالمعنى راضية بالثواب مرضية عنك في الأعمال

rows.speaker: رسول الله
rows.claim: After a man recited these verses and Abū Bakr praised them, the Prophet told Abū Bakr that an angel would say these words to him.
rows.anchor: أحسن هذا ! فقال عليه الصلاة والسلام

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One reported occasion identifies the verse as revealed concerning Ḥamza ibn ʿAbd al-Muṭṭalib.
rows.anchor: قيل : نزلت في حمزة بن عبد المطلب

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another report concerns Khubayb ibn ʿAdī, crucified by Meccans; after he prayed for his face to turn toward God’s city, God turned it and no one could turn it back.
rows.anchor: في خبيب بن عدي الذي صلبه أهل مكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although specific occasions are reported, the lesson follows the wording’s generality rather than a particular cause.
rows.anchor: أن العبرة بعموم اللفظ لا بخصوص السبب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Entering among God’s servants means joining His servants brought near to Him, a noble state.
rows.anchor: إلى عبادي المقربين ،   وهذه حالة شريفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Pure souls resemble polished mirrors; when joined, they reflect one another’s rays, increasing spiritual bliss and rank.
rows.anchor: الأرواح الشريفة القدسية تكون كالمرايا المصقولة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This joining and its spiritual happiness are illustrated by the greeting to those on the right.
rows.anchor: من قوله تعالى : { وأما إن كان من أصحاب اليمين فسلام لك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Entering God’s garden here indicates bodily happiness.
rows.anchor: وهذا إشارة إلى السعادة الجسمانية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The spiritual garden is attained immediately after death, so it follows with fa; bodily Paradise comes only after the great Resurrection, so it follows with wa.
rows.anchor: ولما كانت الجنة الروحانية غير متراخية عن الموت في حق السعداء

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abū ʿUbayda derives lubad from piling things together and takes it to mean great wealth piled up.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عبيدة : لبد ،   فعل من التلبيد

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj says this form indicates abundance, as in ḥaṭim for someone who breaks much.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج : فعل للكثرة يقال رجل حطم

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ says the singular is labda and lubad is its plural, though some treat lubad as singular; either way it denotes much.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء : واحدته لبدة ولبد جمع

rows.speaker: الليث
rows.claim: Al-Layth glosses it as wealth so abundant that one does not fear its running out.
rows.anchor: قال الليث : مال لبد لا يخاف فناؤه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The disbeliever boasts that he spent greatly in hostility toward Muḥammad, on what pre-Islamic Arabs called generosity, nobility, and glory.
rows.anchor: أن هذا الكافر يقول : أهلكت في عداوة محمد مالا كثيرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After reporting the disbeliever’s question about whether anyone sees him, God points to the creation of his eyes as evidence of divine power.
rows.anchor: لما حكى عن ذلك الكافر قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The extraordinary properties of bodily organs are discussed in books of anatomy.
rows.anchor: وعجائب هذه الأعضاء مذكورة في كتب التشريح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Najd is an elevated road; clear proofs are like a high road plainly visible to the eyes, and most exegetes take the two roads as good and evil.
rows.anchor: النجد الطريق في ارتفاع فكأنه لما وضحت الدلائل

rows.speaker: أبي هريرة
rows.claim: Abū Hurayra reports the Prophet saying the two roads are the road of good and the road of evil, and that no one should prefer evil’s road.
rows.anchor: وعن أبي هريرة أنه عليه السلام قال : «إنما هما النجدان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse parallels the passage on human creation with hearing and sight and guidance to the two paths, whether grateful or ungrateful.
rows.anchor: وهذه الآية كالآية في : { هل أتى على الإنسان }

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ḥasan says the boast asks who will hold the spender accountable; the answer is the One who created his organs.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن : قال { أهلكت مالا لبدا }

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وسعيد بن المسيب
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās and Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib interpret the two elevated paths as the two breasts, paths of a child’s life and provision.
rows.anchor: وروي عن ابن عباس وسعيد بن المسيب ،   أنهما الثديان

rows.speaker: القفال
rows.claim: Al-Qaffāl prefers the interpretation that the two paths are the paths of good and evil.
rows.anchor: قال القفال : والتأويل هو الأول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The One who made a rational heart and eloquent tongue from humble fluid can destroy what He created and knows what creatures conceal; denying God and spending against His religion have no excuse.
rows.anchor: إن من قدر على أن يخلق من الماء المهين قلبا عقولا

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ treats ṭughyān and ṭughwā as verbal nouns, with ṭughwā chosen because it better suits the verse endings, like daʿwā from duʿāʾ.
rows.anchor: قال الفراء : الطغيان والطغوى مصدران

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The well-known reading is that their transgression caused them to disbelieve, like saying someone wronged another through audacity against God.
rows.anchor: كما تقول : ظلمني بجراءته على الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second reading takes ṭughwā as their extraordinary punishment: they denied the punishment their messenger had warned them about.
rows.anchor: أن الطغوى اسم لعذابهم الذي أهلكوا به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The punishment reading is plausible because ṭughyān means exceeding the ordinary limit; the exceptional cry could be called ṭughwā, as in references to the calamity and overpowering punishment.
rows.anchor: ويدل على هذا التأويل قوله تعالى : { كذبت ثمود وعاد بالقارعة }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The messenger is Ṣāliḥ; when he learned they intended to hamstring the she-camel, he named it as God’s sign of oneness and his prophethood and warned them not to harm it or deny its water.
rows.anchor: المراد من الرسول صالح عليه السلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The camel had a drinking day and the people and livestock another; burdened by this, they intended to kill her, while Ṣāliḥ repeatedly warned of punishment, so the brief allusion sufficed.
rows.anchor: وقد بينا في مواضع من هذا الكتاب أنه كان لها شرب يوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nāqata Allāh is an accusative warning construction, like repeating “the lion” or “the child,” with omitted commands to leave her unharmed and protect her watering right.
rows.anchor: ناقة الله } نصب على التحذير ،   كقولك الأسد الأسد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They did not refrain from denying Ṣāliḥ and killing the she-camel despite God’s warning of punishment.
rows.anchor: ثم بين تعالى أن القوم لم يمتنعوا عن تكذيب صالح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qudār may have performed the killing directly, while the deed is also attributed to the group because they approved it; the direct attribution is paralleled elsewhere.
rows.anchor: ثم يجوز أن يكون المباشر للعقر واحدا وهو قدار

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says the people would not kill the she-camel until young and old, men and women, had pledged to do so; this was the majority view of exegetes.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة : ذكر لنا أنه أبى أن يعقرها

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ reports the view that there were two perpetrators.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء : قيل إنهما كانا اثنين

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj glosses damdama as enclosing them with punishment; repeated application covers them all around, like something smeared over every side.
rows.anchor: قال الزجاج : معنى دمدم أطبق عليهم العذاب

rows.speaker: الواحدي
rows.claim: Al-Wāḥidī says dam means smearing or staining, and a fat thing is described as though smeared with fat.
rows.anchor: قال الواحدي : الدم في اللغة اللطخ

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjāj derives the doubled form like kabkabū and explains it as punishment enveloping everyone, as a coating stains an object on all sides.
rows.anchor: فجعل الزجاج دمدم من هذا الحرف على التضعيف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Damdama can mean burying or leveling over them, so the earth was smoothed over them after they were killed and placed beneath the soil.
rows.anchor: تقول للشيء : يدفن دمدمت عليه ،   أي سويت عليه

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbārī says damdama means anger, and it can mean speech that agitates a man.
rows.anchor: قال ابن الأنباري : دمدم غضب

rows.speaker: ثعلب
rows.claim: Thaʿlab transmits from Ibn al-Aʿrābī, in agreement with Al-Farrāʾ, that it means the earth shook over them.
rows.anchor: أرجف الأرض بهم رواه ثعلب عن ابن الأعرابي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If damdama means enveloping punishment, fasawwāhā means that the punishment covered everyone equally: Gabriel’s cry killed them, young and old alike.
rows.anchor: إن فسرنا الدمدمة بالإطباق والعموم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If damdama means leveling, fasawwāhā means that the earth was leveled over them.
rows.anchor: وإن فسرناها بالتسوية ،   كان المراد فسوى عليهم الأرض

rows.speaker: القفال
rows.claim: Al-Qaffāl says the sūra was revealed about Abū Bakr’s spending for Muslims and Umayya ibn Khalaf’s miserliness and disbelief.
rows.anchor: قال القفال رحمه الله : نزلت هذه السورة في أبي بكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Despite that reported occasion, the sūra’s meaning is general, as its statements that human striving differs and that a blazing fire is warned of show.
rows.anchor: إلا أنها وإن كانت كذلك لكن معانيها عامة للناس

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: ʿAlī reports that at a funeral the Prophet said God knows every soul’s place in Paradise or Hell; when asked whether to rely on this, he said to act, since each is facilitated for what they were created for.
rows.anchor: ويروى عن علي عليه السلام أنه قال : «خرجنا مع رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: At night animals return to their shelters, creation rests from activity, and sleep covers them as rest for bodies and nourishment for spirits.
rows.anchor: أقسم بالليل الذي يأوي فيه كل حيوان إلى مأواه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When day appears, its light removes darkness and people move for livelihood, while birds leave nests and vermin leave hiding places.
rows.anchor: لأن النهار إذا جاء انكشف بضوئه ما كان في الدنيا من الظلمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternating night and day serves human welfare: perpetual night prevents livelihood and perpetual day removes rest, as other verses state.
rows.anchor: فلو كان الدهر كله ليلا لتعذر المعاش ولو كان كله نهارا لبطلت الراحة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The object of يغشى is omitted; it may be the sun, following another oath, “by the night when it covers her.”
rows.anchor: فهو إما الشمس من قوله : { والليل إذا يغشاها }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively the omitted object is the day, as in the wording that night and day cover one another.
rows.anchor: وإما النهار من قوله : { يغشى الليل والنهار }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third possibility is that night covers everything it veils with darkness.
rows.anchor: وإما كل شيء يواريه بظلامه من قوله : { إذا وقب }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The paired descriptions explain how differing deeds lead to good or bad outcomes, reward or punishment.
rows.anchor: ثم إنه سبحانه بين معنى اختلاف الأعمال فيما قلناه من العاقبة المحمودة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading is spending wealth in every good cause, such as freeing slaves and captives and strengthening Muslims against enemies, whether obligatory or voluntary; Abū Bakr did so.
rows.anchor: أن يكون المراد إنفاق المال في جميع وجوه الخير من عتق الرقاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This broad sense parallels the Qurʾānic description of believers spending from what God provided, whether obligatory or voluntary.
rows.anchor: وإطلاق هذا كالإطلاق في قوله : { ومما رزقناهم ينفقون }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reading includes giving the rights of wealth and of the self through obedience; Arabic usage also says someone “gave obedience.”
rows.anchor: أن قوله : { أعطى } يتناول إعطاء حقوق المال وإعطاء حقوق النفس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taqwā means guarding oneself against everything improper; Rāzī refers to his earlier discussion of whether avoiding minor sins is required.
rows.anchor: فهو إشارة إلى الاحتراز عن كل مالا ينبغي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation is lā ilāha illā Allāh: giving and avoiding prohibitions do not benefit without faith in divine unity and prophecy.
rows.anchor: أنها قول لا إله إلا الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation is the good in God’s prescribed bodily and financial acts of worship: one gives for God, avoids prohibitions, and affirms the laws’ beneficial purposes.
rows.anchor: أن الحسنى عبارة عما فرضه الله تعالى من العبادات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third interpretation is God’s promised replacement for spending; the giver trusts that promise, and the replacement exceeds what was spent.
rows.anchor: أن الحسنى هو الخلف الذي وعده الله في قوله

rows.speaker: أبي الدرداء
rows.claim: Abū al-Dardāʾ reports that two angels call each sunset for all creation except humans and jinn: God, replace what the spender gave and bring loss to the one who withholds.
rows.anchor: وروي عن أبي الدرداء أنه قال : «ما من يوم غربت فيه الشمس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the replacement interpretation, denying the promise means withholding wealth through a bad opinion of God; a proverb says withholding what one has reflects such mistrust.
rows.anchor: فبخل بماله لسوء ظنه بالمعبود ، كما قال بعضهم : منع الموجود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A fourth interpretation is the reward, or Paradise; the two explanations amount to the same thing.
rows.anchor: وقيل : إنه الجنة ، والمعنى واحد

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says the person believed God’s promise and acted for that reward.
rows.anchor: قال قتادة : صدق بموعود الله فعمل لذلك الموعود

rows.speaker: القفال
rows.claim: Al-Qaffāl says al-ḥusnā encompasses every good quality, as verses use it for good outcomes, increased reward, and good recompense.
rows.anchor: قال القفال : وبالجملة أن الحسنى لفظة تسع كل خصلة حسنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view takes al-yusrā as Paradise, while another takes it as good and al-ʿusrā as disbelief.
rows.anchor: وجوه ( أحدها ) : أنها الجنة ( وثانيها ) : أنها الخير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further view is that God makes every commanded act and avoidance easy for the person, while the opposite is made difficult.
rows.anchor: أن يسهل عليه كل ما كلف به من الأفعال والتروك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view is an easy return to the person’s earlier obedience, such as renewed spending for God; al-ʿusrā is a return to withholding and denying financial rights.
rows.anchor: اليسرى هي العود إلى الطاعة التي أتى بها أولا

rows.speaker: القفال
rows.claim: Al-Qaffāl explains the metaphor through outcomes: actions ending in ease, rest, and good are yusrā and describe obedience; those ending in hardship and toil are ʿusrā and describe sins.
rows.anchor: قال القفال : ولكل هذه الوجوه مجاز من اللغة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The feminine can refer to a group of actions; for one act it can refer to an implied feminine noun such as trait or deed, and under the return reading to return itself.
rows.anchor: رجع التأنيث إلى الخلة أو الفعلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the feminine refers to an implied path: the easy way and the difficult way.
rows.anchor: أن يكون مرجع التأنيث إلى الطريقة فكأنه قال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because worship is physically strenuous but Paradise makes the effort easy to bear, Paradise itself is called yusrā; expecting it also explains ease in worship.
rows.anchor: إذا علم المكلف أنها تفضي إلى الجنة سهلت تلك الأفعال الشاقة عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If yusrā means Paradise, facilitation means God admits people to it easily and honorably, as passages describe angels greeting them at entry.
rows.anchor: بإدخال الله تعالى إياهم في الجنة بسهولة وإكرام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If yusrā means good works, facilitation is making them active and easy, without the laziness that affects hypocrites and those who show off.
rows.anchor: فالتيسير لها هو تسهيلها على من أراد حتى لا يعتريه

rows.speaker: الأصحاب
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī’s Ashʿarī associates infer divine enabling and withholding: God gives the believer special enabling by making obedience outweigh disobedience for him.
rows.anchor: استدل الأصحاب بهذه الآية على صحة قولهم في التوفيق والخذلان
